task.title: Fix payment client timeouts
task.description: Payment requests intermittently time out under load. Propose a safe fix consistent with the existing retry constraints.

proposal.summary: Bound client timeouts, preserve existing retry limits, restrict retries to transient errors on idempotent/keyed requests, add jittered backoff within a total deadline, validate connection pooling under load, and add attempt-level observability behind a feature flag.
plan_steps: Read current client timeout, retry, backoff, and pooling configuration and record values before changing them.
Implement C1-C5 behind a flag per C7.
Add tests described in each claim verification field.
Run a load test comparing timeout rate, p95/p99 latency, attempt count, and pool saturation flag-off vs flag-on.

claims.statement: Connect and per-request timeouts will be configured separately with a finite total deadline; no timeout will be removed or set to infinite.
Total retry attempts will not exceed the existing configured maximum; the change will not increase maxAttempts.

Retries will occur only for transient connect/timeout/429/5xx errors and, for payment creation, only when an idempotency key is supplied; other 4xx errors and keyless payment creates will make a single attempt.
Retry backoff will be exponential with jitter, honour Retry-After if present, and total backoff plus attempts will be bounded by the total deadline in C1.
HTTP keep-alive/connection pooling will be enabled or its bounded pool size validated against load, with pool wait time and saturation exposed as metrics.
Each attempt will emit structured logs/metrics for timeout type, attempt number, latency, and pool wait, without logging payment credentials or raw idempotency keys.
The change will be deployed behind a feature flag with rollback by disabling the flag, without a data migration.

Payment creation is not assumed idempotent without an idempotency key.

items.description: Unsupported core assumption: no repository, retry code location, base, cap, attempt indexing, attempt-limit value, or existing tests were provided. The proposal itself says it is unknown whether the current backoff already has a cap, contradicting the premise that cappedBackoff is an existing min(cap, base * 2^attempt) value.

The stated interval [cappedBackoff/2, cappedBackoff) depends on unspecified Uniform endpoint semantics, numeric type, rounding, and division behavior in an unknown language. If Uniform includes its upper endpoint or integer/float rounding occurs, the actual delay can equal cappedBackoff; if cappedBackoff is 0 or very small/quantized, the interval degenerates. No edge-case handling is specified for zero, odd, minimum, capped, or overflowing base * 2^attempt values.

Regression risk: the formula lowers the expected delay to 0.75 * cappedBackoff and permits delays as low as 0.5 * cappedBackoff. The proposal does not address total retry-window/deadline budget, downstream load during outages, provider rate limits, or Retry-After requirements, any of which could be affected by systematically shorter retries.

The attempt-limit value is unknown, so preservation alone does not establish compliance with the retrieved 3-attempt constraint. That constraint also has integrity=Invalid, so it cannot be treated as verified documentation; neither compliance nor conflict can be established from the provided evidence.

Byte-for-byte unchanged attempt counting and termination are asserted without the existing code or a snapshot/golden test of pre-change delays and counting. Editing the delay calculation in the unknown retry code creates an unverified risk of attempt-index or off-by-one changes, including sleeping after the final attempt; no explicit no-delay-after-final-attempt test is specified.

Different delays for the same attempt number are not guaranteed by the proposal as written: a deterministically seeded or repeatedly reseeded injectable source, cappedBackoff of 0, or coarse duration quantization can produce identical delays. Production entropy/seeding requirements and a non-degeneracy test criterion are not specified.

Only expected delay is monotonic; realized jittered delays for successive attempts can overlap and decrease because each draw ranges over half of its cappedBackoff. The claim also assumes positive base, monotonic cappedBackoff, and no overflow/truncation, none of which are evidenced. Tests distinguishing expected monotonicity from per-call non-monotonicity are not specified.

Concurrent safety is asserted without naming the standard-library random source or language. Several standard-library random generator instances are not safe for concurrent use without synchronization, while injectable per-call sources can introduce data races. No race-detector, shared-source contention, or synchronization test is specified.

An injectable sleep function creates regression risk around context cancellation, deadlines, and interruption during the jittered sleep; no cancellation/deadline behavior or test is specified. A fake or misconfigured sleeper reaching production could also bypass real waiting.

Security/availability risk: standard-library non-cryptographic randomness can be predictable, and identical default seeding across instances can correlate retry timing and recreate synchronized retry bursts. The proposal gives no per-instance seed independence requirement or cross-instance decorrelation test.

Unchanged retryable-error classification, results, and idempotency-key reuse are asserted without the existing code, an error-classification matrix, key-generation/reuse evidence, or payment outcome tests. Shorter average delays can change timing relative to settlement and idempotency-key lifetime, creating duplicate-payment or changed-outcome risk that delay-only reasoning does not exclude.

The proposal does not state how jitter interacts with non-retryable errors, immediate success/failure returns, server-supplied Retry-After, or overall operation timeout. Regression tests for those paths are only generically mentioned and not enumerated.

Sensitive-data exclusion is unsupported because existing logging conventions and logger-attached context are unknown. New retry logs using an existing payment logger could inherit credentials, card data, or payload fields unless an explicit field allowlist and log-capture/redaction test are used; neither is specified.

Metric design risk is unaddressed: recording actual jittered delay as a metric label rather than a histogram observation would create high cardinality, while logging every retry can amplify volume during outages. No metric type, label set, sampling, or log/metric assertion test is specified.

Traceability is ambiguous: the plan says to add retry timing observability per C7, but in the provided claims observability is claim-8 and claim-7 covers retry semantics. The plan also references C1 for the jitter calculation while the provided formula is claim-2, leaving requirement-to-claim mapping unclear.

task.description: Replace fixed-delay payment retries with exponential backoff while staying within the documented attempt limit.

Retry delays grow exponentially with attempt number using delay = min(cap, base * 2^(retry_index-1)) plus bounded jitter, replacing the fixed delay.
Only transient payment failures are retried; permanent failures such as invalid card details or explicit declines are returned without additional attempts.
All retries for one payment reuse the same idempotency key and payment identifier so a retry cannot create a duplicate charge.
Retry execution respects cancellation and overall deadlines and does not schedule a retry that would exceed them.

The stated formula delay = min(cap, base * 2^(retry_index-1)) plus bounded jitter can exceed the cap whenever jitter is added after the min() operation. The claim of a capped delay is therefore internally inconsistent unless jitter is included before capping or separately bounded within the cap.

task.title: Alert on payment retry bursts
task.description: Operators want an alert when a payment request needs more than 5 retry attempts. Propose the alert and justify the threshold.

proposal.summary: The threshold is taken directly from the operator requirement in the task description. No production retry distribution, retry-policy maximum, baseline rate, or alert-history evidence was provided, so a statistical justification for 5 cannot be claimed from the available evidence; the threshold requires validation against historical data before production paging is relied on.
plan_steps: Define or confirm a per-request retry count derived from retry events grouped by payment request ID.
Implement the alert rule with condition retry_count > 5, severity warning pending operator confirmation, and deduplication by request ID.
Add notification fields listed in claim C3 and link the notification to an operator runbook for retry-burst investigation.
Test the boundary cases 5 and 6 retries and the deduplication case in claims C1, C2, and C4.
Review historical retry distribution, if available, and tune severity, grouping, or rate-based aggregation before enabling production paging.

claims.statement: The alert condition is retry_count > 5 for a single payment request, so it first triggers on the 6th retry attempt for that request.
The alert fires once per request ID on crossing the threshold, rather than once per retry after the threshold.
Each alert notification contains request ID, service name, retry count, first and latest retry timestamps, and downstream error or reason if available.
Alerts at or below 5 retries do not notify operators.
The 5-retry threshold is not validated against normal retry behaviour until baseline data is reviewed.

assumptions: A per-request identifier exists to group retry events for the same payment request.
Retry events or a retry-count metric are emitted by the payment service and are queryable by the alerting system.

task.description: Duplicate charges were reported after retries. Propose adding idempotency keys to payment requests.

proposal.summary: The proposal addresses duplicate charges reported after retries by having clients send a reusable idempotency key per payment intent, having the server atomically claim that key before charging, replaying the stored response for identical duplicates, rejecting payload mismatches, and handling concurrent and crash cases. Each element is stated as a checkable claim with a concrete verification step.

Add the idempotency record table with the uniqueness scope, request hash, state, stored response, payment reference, and expiry, enforced by a database unique constraint.
Implement atomic key claiming before any provider call, payload-hash comparison, stored-response replay, and pending-state handling for concurrent requests.
Implement failure semantics distinguishing unconfirmed failures from confirmed charges, and forward a deterministic provider idempotency token if supported.
Wire client retry logic to generate one key per payment intent and reuse it across retries.

claims.statement: Payment clients generate one cryptographically random idempotency key per distinct payment intent, reuse that exact key on every retry of that intent, and generate a new key for a new payment intent.
The payment-creation endpoint accepts an Idempotency-Key header, rejects keys that are empty or exceed a documented maximum length with HTTP 400, and does not execute a charge for a rejected key.
The server persists idempotency records keyed by a uniqueness scope of (authenticated account, idempotency key) with a database unique constraint on that pair.

Before executing a charge, the server atomically claims the idempotency key by inserting a record containing a hash of the canonical request method, path, and body, a state of pending, and creation and expiry timestamps.

A retry with a previously completed key and an identical request hash returns the originally stored HTTP status and response body, including the original payment identifier, without calling the payment provider again.
A request reusing a completed or pending key with a different request hash is rejected with HTTP 409 or 422 and does not execute a charge or modify the stored record.

Concurrent duplicate requests with the same key and identical payload result in exactly one provider charge; non-executing duplicates either wait for and return the completed response or receive a documented in-progress response such as HTTP 409 with Retry-After.

If processing fails before a charge is confirmed, the idempotency record is either removed or marked retryable so the same key can complete the payment; if a charge was confirmed, the record stores the final response for replay.

Where the payment provider supports its own idempotency mechanism, the server forwards a provider idempotency token derived deterministically from the stored record so a server crash between provider call and local persistence does not cause a second provider charge on retry.
Idempotency records are retained for at least 24 hours after creation and are deletable only after expiry by a cleanup process that does not delete pending or unexpired records.
Duplicate replay, payload-mismatch, and in-progress events emit metrics and structured logs containing a hashed or truncated key and the payment identifier, without logging full payment credentials.

task.title: Add jitter to payment retries
task.description: Retry storms align under load. Add randomized jitter to the existing payment retry backoff without changing the attempt limit.

proposal.summary: Modify only the payment retry delay calculation to apply bounded equal jitter to the existing backoff, preserving the existing backoff ceiling and attempt limit while spreading retry times.
plan_steps: Locate the existing payment retry backoff calculation and its sleep or scheduler call site in the codebase.
Introduce or reuse an injectable random-source dependency at that delay calculation point.
Replace the directly scheduled deterministic backoff with the bounded equal-jitter calculation defined in C2 while retaining the existing backoff and cap from C1.
Confirm through diff inspection that the attempt limit, retry eligibility, attempt counting, and payment execution logic are untouched.
Add deterministic unit tests, bound or property tests, and a persistent-failure attempt-count test using a fake sleeper or clock.
Run the existing payment retry test suite and any relevant concurrency tests.

claims.statement: For retry attempt n, the implementation first computes base_n with the existing backoff formula and existing cap, without changing that formula, its inputs, or the cap.
The scheduled retry delay uses equal jitter: delay_n = base_n/2 + uniform_random(0, base_n/2), so delay_n is always in the interval [base_n/2, base_n].
A fresh random value is drawn independently for each retry attempt and for each payment operation rather than reusing one cached jitter value across retries or operations.
The maximum number of payment attempts, including the existing attempt limit and attempt-counting location, is unchanged.
The jitter change affects only the delay before a retry; it does not change retry eligibility, error classification, payment payloads, idempotency keys, or success and failure handling.
The delay calculation never produces a negative duration, never exceeds base_n, and is applied through the existing sleep or scheduler mechanism without adding a new retry loop.
The random source used in production is the platform or existing project-approved thread-safe random generator, and it is injectable or seedable in tests.

assumptions: The payment retry path already computes a non-negative backoff duration, enforces an attempt limit, and uses an existing sleep or scheduler mechanism.
Jitter is only intended to desynchronize retry timing; it is not intended to change which errors are retryable.
uncertainties: No codebase, file paths, programming language, current backoff formula, cap value, numeric attempt limit, random-generator utility, or test framework was provided, so those implementation-specific details cannot be named or verified here.
Whether base_n can be zero and how the existing code handles zero-duration delays were not provided, so the implementation must follow the existing behavior for that edge case.
